history: The first generation Honda Civic arrived in North America in 1972 as one of the most significant automobiles in automotive history. At a time when the American market was dominated by large, thirsty V8-powered cars, the Civic offered something radical: a lightweight, front-wheel-drive compact with a transversely mounted engine that delivered exceptional fuel economy without sacrificing reliability or driving enjoyment.

Honda's timing proved impeccable. The 1973 oil crisis sent American consumers scrambling for fuel-efficient alternatives, and the Civic was perfectly positioned to capitalize. Its 1.2-liter four-cylinder engine, while modest by any performance measure, delivered real-world fuel economy that domestic manufacturers couldn't match — reportedly achieving over 40 miles per gallon in careful driving.

What made the first-gen Civic remarkable wasn't raw performance but engineering innovation. Honda's CVCC (Compound Vortex Controlled Combustion) engine, introduced in 1975, was the first to meet the strict U.S. Clean Air Act emissions standards without requiring a catalytic converter — a genuine engineering breakthrough that demonstrated Honda's technical capabilities to the world.

The first generation Civic established Honda as a serious global automaker and laid the philosophical foundation for everything that followed. Its emphasis on efficiency, reliability, and value for money created a template that the Civic has followed for over 50 years — making the humble first-gen one of the most historically significant compact cars ever built.
did_you_know: The first-gen Civic's CVCC engine was so clean that Honda sent a letter to the U.S. Senate in 1972 — before the car even launched — claiming it could meet the 1975 Clean Air Act standards that automakers like GM, Ford, and Chrysler were lobbying Congress to delay. Honda was right, and it changed the industry.

trims.name: Civic Base
trims.description: The entry-level Civic in two-door hatchback form with the 1.2L engine, 4-speed manual, and a spartan but functional interior focused entirely on efficiency and value.

trims.name: Civic 1500 GL
trims.description: The top-tier trim featuring the CVCC 1.5L engine, upgraded interior with additional sound deadening, and a more complete feature set including a rear defroster and upgraded seats.

trims.name: Civic CVCC
trims.description: The landmark CVCC-equipped variant that proved a small engine could meet strict emissions standards without sacrificing reliability. Available in sedan and hatchback body styles.

trims.name: Civic Wagon
trims.description: A practical station wagon variant introduced in the final year of the first generation, previewing Honda's expansion of the Civic into multiple body styles in subsequent generations.

variants.name: Civic Hatchback
variants.description: The iconic two-door hatchback that defined the first-gen Civic's image. Its practical rear hatch, light weight, and tossable handling made it a favorite among economy-minded enthusiasts despite its modest power output.

variants.name: Civic Sedan
variants.description: A more formal four-door sedan variant offering greater practicality for families. Less sporty in appearance than the hatchback but mechanically identical, it broadened the Civic's appeal considerably.

variants.name: Honda Accord (Successor Spirit)
variants.description: While not a Civic variant, the Honda Accord was introduced in 1976 as a larger sibling to the first-gen Civic, sharing its front-wheel-drive philosophy and CVCC engine technology — a direct product of the Civic's success.
